- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts show gradual upward drift, correct for overconfidence by reducing slope slightly and adding early volatility buffer.
- If recent events show high bearish net supply (supply_net < -1.0) and forecast is rising, apply downward bias correction — especially if true outcome spikes downward after initial rise.
- After a sharp price spike (true > 85), model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope for next 5 days and add 1–2% downward adjustment to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is neutral or negative (≤0.33) and forecast is rising, flag as “mean reversion risk” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day until sentiment turns.
- If model forecasts are flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows strong volatility (e.g., >10% swing), apply “sentiment-driven volatility filter” — adjust forecast to match sentiment variance (e.g., if sentiment = 0.33, allow ±2% deviation).
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from mean of last 10 days, apply “mean reversion correction” — pull forecast toward historical mean unless sentiment strongly bullish.
- If official event count is high (≥20) and supply_net is negative, model tends to overestimate bullishness — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per event beyond 15.
- When sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model often misreads trend — apply “cycle smoothing” — average last 3 sentiment values to adjust forecast direction.
